title: Doctor 'enraged' over NHS transgender ward policy

input.lead: A consultant psychiatrist says a patient exposed themselves to female patients on the women-only ward
input.summary: A consultant psychiatrist says a patient exposed themselves to female patients on the women-only ward
input.evidence_text: North West health correspondent Published 1 hour ago A row has erupted over NHS policies which allow transgender women onto women-only wards A consultant psychiatrist at Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust (GMMH) claims a patient, who identified as a trans woman, exposed themselves to female patients during their stay Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust (GMMH) said it had investigated the allegations and had no record of this ever happening The case highlights the fact that the NHS still has no national policy reflecting legal changes which say single-sex services must reflect biological sex Earlier this month, The Times reported that the psychiatrist, who has not been named, had filed a tribunal claim with the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service (Acas) in August , external She said she had raised repeated concerns with GMMH over its trans inclusion policies, which are likely to be in breach of a Supreme Court ruling given 17 months ago

title: Manchester Sikh riders mark 50 years of motorcycle helmet exemption

input.lead: The ride honours Gyani Sundar Singh Sagar, imprisoned for refusing to wear a motorcycle crash helmet
input.summary: The ride honours Gyani Sundar Singh Sagar, imprisoned for refusing to wear a motorcycle crash helmet
input.evidence_text: Manchester Sikh riders mark 50 years of motorcycle helmet exemption - BBC News Image caption, Members of the Sikh Motorcycle Club gathered at Strangeways Prison to honour Gyani Sundar Singh Sagar By Kaya Black and Haider Saleem , Reporting from North West Published 1 hour ago About 20 Sikh motorcyclists have taken part in a ride marking 50 years since a Manchester Sikh campaigner helped secure a change to motorcycle helmet laws. The group travelled from Strangeways Prison, near Manchester city centre, to the Sikh temple Sri Guru Gobind Singh Gurdwara in the south of the city in honour of campaigner Gyani Sundar Singh Sagar. Known as Gyani Ji, he spent a week in Strangeways in 1976 for refusing to pay fines for riding his moped while wearing a turban instead of a crash helmet, his son Bharat Sagar said. Another son, Ujjal Singh, who was there when he was released, said returning to the spot 50 years later was "quite nostalgic" and he was proud his father's legacy lived on. His sons said he got straight back on his moped after leaving prison and was stopped six more times by police within a short distance. A replica of Gyani Ji's moped was displayed as riders and members of his family gathered outside the prison before setting off on the memorial ride. Image source, Supplied Image caption, Gyani Sundar Singh Sagar was better known as Gyani Ji Bharat, 67, said he felt "incredibly proud for being a Sikh, but more proud for being a Mancunian". "I think this is as much a Manchester thing and a societal thing as it is just a Sikh thing," he said. "It's more about tolerance and creating a better, wider society." title: Manchester to host world leaders at G20 summit in 2027

title: Manchester man who confessed to 1994 masked gang murder jailed

input.lead: Robert Lloyd, now 53, walked into a police station earlier this year to confess the brutal killing
input.summary: Robert Lloyd, now 53, walked into a police station earlier this year to confess the brutal killing
input.evidence_text: Manchester man who confessed to 1994 masked gang murder jailed - BBC News Image source, Greater Manchester Police Image caption, Robert Lloyd has been sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of Michael McDermott in 1994 By Rebecca Brahde North West Published 21 September 2026 A man who walked into a police station and confessed to a murder more than 30 years ago has been sentenced to life imprisonment. Robert Lloyd, now 53, was part of a group of masked men who attacked Michael McDermott, 26, at his relative's home in Moston, Manchester, on 9 November 1994. Armed with baseball bats and knives, the offenders burst through the front door of the property at about 22:30 GMT. They inflicted several injuries on McDermott, including stab wounds, as he lay on the sofa. Lloyd was jailed at Manchester Crown Court for a minimum of 17 years in March, but reporting restrictions had previously been in place due to ongoing police inquiries. Following the attack at the house in Ashville Terrace, the group ran across the road to an alleyway and on to Oakville Terrace to a waiting vehicle which then drove them from the scene. Image source, Greater Manchester Police Image caption, Michael McDermott, 26, was attacked as he was laying on the sofa The case was reopened by Greater Manchester Police's major investigation team last October after Lloyd, from Denton, Tameside, confessed. He subsequently pleaded guilty to the charge of murder in March. Det Insp Rachel Smith said: "Michael's death 30 years ago was devastating for his loved ones and has left unanswered questions ever since. "It is my hope that Michael's family feels a sense of reassurance and peace after this sentencing." The police investigation remains ongoing as detectives work to identify other individuals involved in the

title: Health worker 'kissed and touched colleagues' as they cared for patients

input.lead: Stephen Spencer has been struck off for "crossing boundaries" with his female colleagues
input.summary: Stephen Spencer has been struck off for "crossing boundaries" with his female colleagues
input.evidence_text: Health worker 'kissed and touched colleagues' as they cared for patients - BBC News Image source, Google Image caption, Stephen Spencer said he was "old school" after colleagues at Wrightington Hospital complained By Jonny Humphries North West Published 21 September 2026 A health clinician has been struck off for kissing and touching his female colleagues as they tried to care for patients. Stephen Spencer, an operating department practitioner at Wrightington Hospital in Appley Bridge, was described as "leery" by one colleague and left another feeling "violated and intimidated". When questioned by his managers he told them the allegations had been "bang out of order" and added: "I'm old school and will always help women." However, Spencer was investigated by regulator the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC) and found guilty of gross misconduct at a tribunal. He was referred to the HCPC by Wrightington, Wigan and Leigh Teaching Hospital NHS Trust after an internal investigation into his conduct. In a written judgment the tribunal panel said the first complainant, referred to as Colleague A, was standing near a patient while working with Spencer in September 2022. The judgment described how he moved from near the head of the patient to where she was standing by their feet. 'Shaken and uncomfortable' The tribunal heard that she "thought that he was going to say something about the patient, but instead he kissed her on her right cheek". The kiss left her feeling "shaken and uncomfortable," Colleague A said. She told the tribunal she was unsure if she was being "oversensitive" so asked a friend and a male colleague, who both agreed it had been inappropriate. title: Manchester Northern Quarter counter-terror arrests

input.lead: The two men were held in Newton Street, Manchester, and remain in custody
input.summary: The two men were held in Newton Street, Manchester, and remain in custody
input.evidence_text: Manchester Northern Quarter counter-terror arrests - BBC News Image caption, The pair were held in Newton Street, Manchester, as part of an ongoing operation By Stewart Whittingham North West Published 21 September 2026 Two men have been arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences after a major police swoop in Manchester's Northern Quarter. The pair were held in Newton Street at 14:45 BST on Sunday as part of an ongoing operation. They remain in custody. Police said a property on Epworth Street in Liverpool had been searched as well as one on Lancaster Road in Salford. The operation was led by the Metropolitan Police and backed up by officers from Greater Manchester Police (GMP). Image caption, Police visited a block of flats on Epworth Street in Liverpool A Counter Terrorism Policing London spokesperson said: "Both males were arrested under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000. "The operation was led by Counter Terrorism Policing London, working closely with Counter Terrorism Policing North West and Greater Manchester Police." They added: "At this time, there is no information to suggest any wider threat to the public." title: Manchester brain health clinic aims to 'transform' dementia care

input.lead: The Alzheimer's Society says the clinic in Manchester is the first of its kind in the United Kingdom
input.summary: The Alzheimer's Society says the clinic in Manchester is the first of its kind in the United Kingdom
input.evidence_text: A brain health clinic seeking to "transform" how dementia is diagnosed, slowed down and treated has opened on World Alzheimer's Day The Manchester Brain Health Centre (MBHC) is located at Manchester Royal Infirmary The first clinic of its kind in the UK, MBHC is bringing together psychiatrists, vascular specialists and academics under a single service to identify and treat memory loss earlier "Right now, the system is not set up for people when memory and thinking problems first appear," said Dr Ross Dunne, dementia research lead at Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust. "That is exactly when early diagnosis and treatment could have the greatest impact He added: "The Manchester Brain Health Centre is crucial to advancing our understanding and treatment of the diseases that cause dementia." MBHC is a two-year pilot spearheaded by the Alzheimer's Society

title: Bring your own booze policy saved my Manchester nightclub, says owner

input.lead: A Manchester nightclub owner says the policy has boosted profits from ticket prices instead
input.summary: A Manchester nightclub owner says the policy has boosted profits from ticket prices instead
input.evidence_text: Bring your own booze policy saved my Manchester nightclub, says owner - BBC News Image caption, XLR club boss Chris Hindle said the policy had been a hit with customers By Lynette Horsburgh North West Published 21 September 2026 A nightclub owner said their idea to allow customers to bring their own alcohol has saved the venue from closing. The XLR nightspot in Withington, Manchester, brought in the unusual policy a year ago. Owner Chris Hindle said it gave the club a "real boost" with more people coming through the doors during what has been a tough financial climate in the hospitality sector. He said relying on ticket sales predominantly has been a "win-win" situation with customers saving money and the club's takings receiving a boost. While "bring your own booze" policies are not unusual in restaurants that do not serve alcohol, nightclubs traditionally rely heavily on their bar takings to survive. The 33-year-old club owner said XLR, which is popular with students, would have folded had he not introduced the policy and customers were happy, too, with the maximum ticket price being £20. "We've had a lot of feedback from customers saying they've saved a lot of money on nights out and, financially, the club's doing well," he said. "If I didn't put it in place, I would have probably had to close the venue down last November. "It has been a real boost for the club's finances. Everybody wins in this situation. "The customers don't have to spend as much money. We save a lot of time and hassle on not buying as much alcohol in, and it just means the club can charge a bit more for the tickets and that's where our profit lies. title: BBC boosts Greater Manchester economy by £450m, broadcaster says

input.summary: BBC activity accounts for 39% of Greater Manchester's production and broadcasting sector, a report says
input.evidence_text: The BBC contributed £450m to Greater Manchester's economy in 2024-25 and supported more than 5,000 jobs, according to a new report The figures have been released as part of the BBC's Made Of Greater Manchester campaign, marking 15 years since the BBC moved key departments to Media City in Salford The report by BBC economists said BBC activity accounted for 39% of the city region's audiovisual production and broadcasting sector and the corporation employed more than 3,000 people However, it warned that future investment could be affected by financial pressures facing public service broadcasters and wider challenges in the production sector Continued growth depended on a sustainable long-term funding settlement, it added The BBC's Economic Impact In Greater Manchester report described the BBC as a "strategic anchor" for the creative industries and said 422 apprentices had been employed in Salford over five years

input.summary: A python has also been recovered from the semi-detached house in Hale, Greater Manchester
input.evidence_text: A "dangerous" crocodilian has been recovered from a suburban home after reports it was being kept without a licence The spectacled caiman, classified as dangerous under the Dangerous Wild Animal Act 1976, was seized from a semi-detached house in Hale, Greater Manchester, on Wednesday Lyle the caiman was found, along with a python, after a Trafford Council-led operation also involving police and the RSPCA. Both animals have since been moved to a zoo, said the council "These animals have highly specialised needs that are incredibly difficult to meet in a domestic setting," said RSPCA exotic animal expert Evie Button. "We're pleased that both reptiles are now receiving specialist care but we remain deeply concerned that so many dangerous wild animals continue to be kept in private hands across Britain," she added The caiman was discovered in an enclosure with water when environmental health officers - along with police and the RSPCA - executed a warrant at the property at about 11:00 BST

Bolton is set to receive over £6.5m, meaning that together with its own funding the council now has a war chest of around £10m to spend on improvements right across the borough. Over 40 hotspots will be targeted for repair by spring of next year. The idea is to tackle roads where surfaces are in poor condition, as well as resurface roads and pavements to prevent them from deteriorating in the first place. Damaged roads are a common gripe for residents and can be dangerous for road users of all kinds - not only car drivers, but also buses, trams, cyclists and pedestrians. Cold and wet winters, more traffic and heavier vehicles are just some of the factors making roads worse. Repair work will be coordinated through the council’s Highways Capital Programme, which was approved in August, and carried out by contactors. It comes as Bolton is benefiting from the fourth highest funding allocation in the ten Greater Manchester authorities after new GM Mayor, Bev Craig, announced a £60m road maintenance fund as one of her first big priorities. The fund is estimated to be enough to repair and maintain over a million square metres – or around 125 kilometres – of road. Bolton Council’s Executive Member for Highways, Transport and Planning, Cllr Nadeem Ayub, said: “This funding is very welcome and will allow us to bring forward work on the roads on our priority list. “We are taking a sensible, planned approach to making our roads better over the long term and I’m confident that residents will start to see improvements soon.” Cookie Consent by Free Privac

input.evidence_text: The new exhibition Laura Knight: The Art of Community opens at Bolton Museum on Saturday 19 September The exhibition brings together the museum’s small but significant collection of works by the pioneering British artist This is the first time that the four paintings and one drawing have been shown together in one gallery Dame Laura Knight (1877-1970) is one of Britain’s best-loved artists whose career spanned 70 years and encompassed a huge variety of subjects, techniques, and styles Her achievements were many: she was the first female artist to be elected as a full member of the Royal Academy, she was a prominent war artist in both World Wars, and she was made a Dame in 1929 for her services to art The exhibition at Bolton Museum includes her celebrated painting, The Fishing Fleet , from 1900, with the dramatic work depicting the working life of the fishing community in Staithes

title: Manchester AI firm reaches £13m ARR - without a sales team

input.lead: A Manchester-based AI-native company that streamlines operational workflows has passed five million cases processed for regulated firms in under three years – built entirely without a sales team, marketing function or paid acquisition.
input.summary: A Manchester-based AI-native company that streamlines operational workflows has passed five million cases processed for regulated firms in under three years – built entirely without a sales team, marketing function or paid acquisition. Saber was founded in January 2024 by Jakub L
input.evidence_text: Manchester AI firm reaches £13m ARR - without a sales team Posted on September 21, 2026 by staff Manchester AI firm reaches £13m ARR – without a sales team Saber, founded by two engineers after a single audit job, now automates correspondence and document work for regulated firms Share: Founders A Manchester-based AI-native company that streamlines operational workflows has passed five million cases processed for regulated firms in under three years – built entirely without a sales team, marketing function or paid acquisition. Saber was founded in January 2024 by Jakub Lenski and Mitchel Shephard after completing a one-off audit for a law firm. Tasked with auditing a 200,000-claim book by hand – a job estimated to take six weeks to complete 10% of – Saber produced a one-off automation workflow that processed the entire book in under three days. Saber has since evolved into a Manchester team of 32 – mostly engineers – and a product that saves 96.3% of time per case. Concerns over AI’s accuracy can be a barrier to adoption, making human oversight a key component of Saber’s design. At a time when 42% of companies abandon most AI initiatives before production, Saber goes live on a real production workflow in approximately two weeks and provides measurable return on investment right from deployment. Lenski puts that down to how the software gets deployed rather than the models themselves. “Most automation projects in regulated sectors take six months to go live,” said Lenski. “By then the workflow has moved on, the team has lost faith, and the original business case is unrecognisable. “We built Saber so the platform is live on a real production workflow within two weeks – and the customer proves the savings on their own data before signing anything commercial.” VCs back InTo
